\chapter{Les --- And What the Second System Costs}
\label{ch:pronoun-les}
\hlchaptermodality{94}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say les digo and name the four pronouns that are identical in both object systems.}

Complete ES-C46-les: produce les digo and say how many genuinely new words the indirect set adds.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[les]{les — \textquotedblleft{}to them,\textquotedblright{} and what this system really costs}

\label{lesson:ES-C46-les}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Lo} became \emph{los}. So what does \emph{le} become? Say it before you read on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: right again, and then something better}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{les} — \emph{to them}, \emph{to you all}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Le digo.} — I tell him. $\to$ \emph{\textbf{Les} digo.} — I tell them.
\end{quote}

Add \emph{-s}. That is the second time an object pronoun has pluralised without argument, and it will not be the last.

Now the part worth the chapter. You have just met the sixth and last indirect object pronoun — and you have only ever been \textbf{taught two of them}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Here are the two sets, side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{direct (\emph{what})} & \textbf{indirect (\emph{to whom})} \\
\midrule
me & \textbf{me} & \textbf{me} \\
you & \textbf{te} & \textbf{te} \\
him / her / you & \textbf{lo}, \textbf{la} & \textbf{le} \\
us & \textbf{nos} & \textbf{nos} \\
you all \emph{(Spain)} & \textbf{os} & \textbf{os} \\
them / you all & \textbf{los}, \textbf{las} & \textbf{les} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Look down the two columns. \textbf{Four of the six rows are identical.} \emph{Me}, \emph{te}, \emph{nos} and \emph{os} do not change at all — the same word does both jobs, and Spanish never asks you to choose.

So a \textquotedblleft{}whole second system\textquotedblright{} turns out to cost exactly \textbf{two new words}: \emph{le} and \emph{les}. Everything else you already owned, and you owned it before you knew there were two systems to own it in.

This is worth holding onto beyond this chapter. A grammar book will show you two complete tables and it will look like twelve things. Count what is actually \textbf{different} and it is two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le digo\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}les digo\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me, te, nos, os\textquotedblright{} and note that this list is finished for both systems at once
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}I tell them\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Les digo}}.) How many new words did the whole indirect system cost you? (\textbf{Two}.) Next: how to know which of the two a verb is asking for.
\end{tcolorbox}
